candidates.title: Show HN: Hubzoid – Turns a folder of Markdown into an AI agent your team can use
candidates.raw_content: Hi HN, Kakshil here, I am building an open-source tool which converts a folder of markdown files into an agent, which can be shared with a team with tool based access control. The main goal with this was to have one "brain" or a folder, which I used to make my local Claude Code agents on, work for my team with checks, and also, run workflows on the server. The same "brain" can be used for a chat agent or a workflow agent or an MCP server. Try with: pip install hubzoid hubzoid init my-agent hubzoid run my-agent Or use one of the ready to use agents, to get started quickly. Details in the readme. It runs on Claude and OpenAI agents SDK, so the harness is borrowed. It's apache 2.0 fully. Docs are here: https://hubzoid.com/docs . It runs with your existing claude or codex subscription, so no other api key needed to try it out. Do try it out and share feedback. Happy to answer any questions. candidates.title: Agent swarms have the potential to drive yet another leap in output from AI. The impact will be a clear separation between teams that adopt this pattern of work and those that don’t. The progression has roughly been: chat gave us quick turn AI responses that let us work a bit faster, but we were still rate limited by our interactions; then agents that can go off and complete entire tasks for us, accelerating hours or days of work into minutes; to now swarms of agents that are goal seeking and will find any route to the successful completion of a project, where there’s no inherent limit to the productivity gains. We can imagine a future where, for any task in which value can be created within a self-contained digital environment, swarms will be able to complete the work faster than any other approach. Essentially any area where value creation is currently bound by the amount of research you can do, the amount of decisions made with a set of software tools, the amount of data processed or consumed, and the amount of code (or code adjacent) that can be generated. This means swarms will play a big role in game development, coding, trading, life sciences research, IT automation, cyber, math breakthroughs, animation, and plenty of other areas of work that have these characteristics. There’s a lot of opportunity to build the harnesses, applied AI products, and infrastructure for how these agents operate. And most importantly there’s a ton of opportunity for those that can wire up work in this way. It’s going to be an entire new field of FDE work available.

candidates.title: BREAKING: @Google just dropped Gemini 4 Carbon. It’s a much better coder than Argon—but I’m probably keeping Argon for writing. We’ve been testing it at @every across coding, writing, design, and knowledge work. It can work for hours on an ambitious project, but it doesn’t always know when to stop. Here’s your day-zero vibe check: • Coding: On one run of our Senior Engineer benchmark, Carbon scored 44%, versus Argon’s 21%. A big improvement, though still middle of the pack. In a separate test, @hammer_mt gave it a backlog to work through. It identified 6 tasks as ready, then did 15—including work someone else was already doing. He stopped it after almost 4.5 hours. • Big builds: @RandyCounsman gave it 3D scans of our podcast studio and an equipment list. In one attempt, it built a browser-based model accurate enough to check whether new gear would fit without getting into the shot. He estimates Carbon also wrote about 95% of a big update to Everycut, our internal video editor. • Code quality: @kieranklaassen values its tests and documentation on large projects, including its record of approaches it considered and rejected. Fable remains his first choice, but Carbon has earned a place alongside it. The catch: It can produce huge files where Fable keeps things more modular. • Audio and video: Randy found it caught audio editing issues other models missed. Kieran handed it a recorded meeting and asked for shorts. It came back with 6 titled clips. • Design: @jackcheng got a hyperrealistic ginkgo-leaf app icon with details other models struggle with. Objects and 3D scenes look better than Argon’s. Interfaces split the team: Jack and Randy kept getting boxes within boxes, while @TylerNishida liked its ideas for new interfaces. Kieran says giving it design guidance makes a big difference. • Writing: Our editorial benchmark put Carbon and Argon about even. If you like Argon, you’ll probably like Carbon. But Carbon costs more, and I haven’t seen enough improvement to justify switching. My Reach Test: 🟨 I’ll use it sometimes. Give it one big job with a clear finish line, and review what comes back. It’s also worth trying as a second opinion, especially on audio and video. Full vibe check coming soon: https://t.co/Ch2pNl9Po5
